description: kube-scheduler: what it schedules, how fast, which plugin or extender decides, health of extenders and of the simulate endpoint, resources of the scheduler pods.

panels.title: Replicas
panels.description:
Every kube-scheduler replica, one row per master node.

- Role: `leader` places pods, `standby` waits to take over. Exactly one leader is normal.
- Scrape: `down` means Prometheus cannot read the replica, so its data is missing from the other panels.
- Version: differs between replicas only during an upgrade.

A replica that is not ready is not scraped and has no row.

panels.title: Pods scheduled
panels.description: How many pods per second kube-scheduler places on nodes, all selected profiles. 0 with an empty queue is normal. 0 while Pending pods grows means scheduling is stuck: check Attempt errors and Unschedulable pods by plugin.

panels.title: Pending pods
panels.description: Pods waiting in the scheduling queue of the leader, including pods that wait for capacity and pods held by scheduling gates. Short peaks that return to 0 are normal. Growth over minutes: see Pending pods by queue for the sub-queue that grows. Standby replicas keep their own copy of the queue; only the leader is counted.

panels.title: Attempt p99
panels.description: 99th percentile of one scheduling attempt, any result: from taking the pod from the queue until the pod is bound to its node or the attempt fails. For placed pods it includes the wait on Permit and the PreBind and Bind steps, e.g. volume provisioning. High values: find the slow step in Scheduling attempt duration and Extension point duration p99. The number shows the last few minutes. It stops at 16.4 s, the top of the histogram: a reading at the cap means longer than that, how much longer is unknown. With fewer than about 100 attempts in the rate window the value is set by the single slowest attempt, rounded up to the top of its bucket, so one pod that waits longer than 16 s for its volume to be created is enough to reach the cap.

panels.title: Attempt errors
panels.description: Scheduling attempts per second that failed with an internal error: an API call failed, a plugin returned an error, or an extender with failure policy Fail did not answer properly. Pods that fit no node are counted separately, as unschedulable in Schedule attempts by result. Any value above 0 needs a look: kube-scheduler logs name the pod and the cause, extender failures are in Error ratio by extender and verb.

panels.title: Schedule attempts by result
panels.description: Scheduling attempts per second by result: `scheduled` placed a pod, `unschedulable` found no node that fits (the pod goes back to the queue), `error` failed internally. Steady `unschedulable` with little `scheduled` means pods wait for capacity: check Unschedulable pods by plugin.

panels.title: Scheduling attempt duration
panels.description: Quantiles of one scheduling attempt, any result, from taking the pod from the queue until binding or failure. The dashed `algorithm p99` covers filtering, scoring and, for attempts that found no node, the search for preemption victims; extender calls included. The gap above it is Reserve, Permit, PreBind and Bind. The gap is a rough estimate because quantiles do not add up. Lines stop at 16.4 s, the top of the histogram: a flat line at the cap means longer than that, how much longer is unknown. With fewer than about 100 attempts in the rate window `p99` is set by the single slowest attempt, rounded up to the top of its bucket: one pod that waits for its volume to be created raises it for one rate window, which gives flat steps a few minutes wide. Compare with `p90`: when `p90` stays low, the scheduler is fine and the outlier is one pod. `algorithm p99` covers all profiles, the Profile selector does not apply to it.

panels.title: Pending pods by queue
panels.description: Pods in the scheduling queue of the leader by sub-queue: `active` waits for the next attempt, `backoff` waits a delay after a failed attempt, `unschedulable` waits for a cluster change that may let it fit, `gated` is held by scheduling gates. Growing `active` means the scheduler does not keep up: check Scheduling attempt duration. Growing `unschedulable` means the cluster has no room for these pods: check Unschedulable pods by plugin.

targets.expr: sum by (queue) (scheduler_pending_pods{job="kube-scheduler", node=~"$node"} * on (instance) group_left () (max by (instance) (leader_election_master_status{job="kube-scheduler", name="kube-scheduler"}) == 1))

panels.title: Pods entering the queue by event
panels.description: Pods per second added to a sub-queue of the leader, by the event that moved them: a new pod, a failed attempt, a new node, and so on. Many `ScheduleAttemptFailure` with few `UnschedulablePodAdd` (`UnscheduledPodAdd` since Kubernetes 1.37) means the same pods are retried again and again: check Unschedulable pods by plugin.

targets.expr: sum by (queue, event) (rate(scheduler_queue_incoming_pods_total{job="kube-scheduler", node=~"$node"}[$__rate_interval]) * on (instance) group_left () (max by (instance) (leader_election_master_status{job="kube-scheduler", name="kube-scheduler"}) == 1))

panels.title: Unschedulable pods by plugin
panels.description: Waiting pods by the plugin that rejected them, e.g. `NodeResourcesFit` (not enough CPU or memory), `NodeAffinity`, `TaintToleration`, `VolumeBinding`. A pod is counted once for every plugin that rejected it, so the lines do not add up to the number of pods. `Extender`: rejected by an extender, see the Extenders row for which one. `SchedulingGates`: pods held by scheduling gates, they wait for whoever set the gate. Only the leader replica is counted: standbys also queue pods with gates.

targets.expr: sum by (plugin) (scheduler_unschedulable_pods{job="kube-scheduler", node=~"$node", profile=~"$profile"} * on (instance) group_left () (max by (instance) (leader_election_master_status{job="kube-scheduler", name="kube-scheduler"}) == 1))

panels.title: Pod scheduling latency (SLI)
panels.description: Time from the pod becoming ready to schedule (scheduling gates removed) until it is bound to a node, across all attempts it needed. Includes waiting after failed attempts and waiting for capacity, so one pod waiting for a new node raises p99. Only placed pods are counted: pods that still wait are in Pending pods.

panels.title: Attempts per scheduled pod
panels.description: How many attempts a placed pod needed. An average close to 1 is normal. A high p99 means some pods fail again and again before they fit: check Unschedulable pods by plugin and Pods entering the queue by event.

panels.title: Preemption
panels.description: `attempts`: preemptions per second, made when a pod fits no node and the scheduler looks for lower-priority pods to evict. `victims`: pods evicted per second to make room. Attempts without victims mean no node had pods worth evicting, or the pod may not preempt, and the pod stays unschedulable. Steady victims mean high-priority pods regularly push out lower-priority ones.

panels.title: Scheduling attempt p99: PreBind, VolumeBinding, whole attempt
panels.description: The 99th percentile of three things on one scale: the whole scheduling attempt that ended with a node (`result=scheduled`), the PreBind extension point, and the VolumeBinding plugin alone. PreBind is part of the binding cycle and counts into the attempt, so a pod that waits there for a volume (a `WaitForFirstConsumer` PVC that the CSI driver has not provisioned yet) makes the attempt as long as the wait. If the attempt line follows PreBind and VolumeBinding, the time goes into volume binding, not into filtering, scoring or extenders. The plugin metrics are recorded for a sample of attempts only, so the VolumeBinding line is a rough estimate. The attempt histogram ends at 16.384 s: when more than 1% of the attempts in the window are longer, the quantile is clamped to that value, so a flat line at 16 s means "at least 16 s". With few attempts per interval one slow attempt is enough: see the attempt rate panel next to this one. The Profile selector does not apply to the VolumeBinding line, the plugin metric has no profile label.

targets.expr: histogram_quantile(0.99, sum by (le) (rate(scheduler_scheduling_attempt_duration_seconds_bucket{job="kube-scheduler", node=~"$node", profile=~"$profile", result="scheduled"}[$__rate_interval])))

panels.title: Scheduling attempts rate
panels.description: Completed scheduling attempts per second by result, counted from the attempt duration histogram (`scheduler_scheduling_attempt_duration_seconds_count`). This is the sample the percentiles of the neighbouring panel and of "Scheduling attempt duration" are computed from: when the rate is low, a single slow attempt moves the p99 by itself, so a spike on the p99 panel next to a few attempts per minute is one pod, not a trend.

panels.title: Extension point duration p99
panels.description: 99th percentile of each step of a scheduling cycle (PreFilter, Filter, Score, Reserve, Permit, PreBind, Bind and others), all plugins of the step together, any result. Filter covers filtering of all nodes of the cycle at once. A slow step points to its plugins in Plugin execution duration p99 (top 15). Extender calls are not part of these steps: see Request latency p50 / p99.

targets.expr: histogram_quantile(0.99, sum by (le, extension_point) (rate(scheduler_framework_extension_point_duration_seconds_bucket{job="kube-scheduler", node=~"$node", profile=~"$profile"}[$__rate_interval])))

panels.title: Plugin execution duration p99 (top 15)
panels.description: 99th percentile of a single plugin at a single step, the 15 slowest. Sampled: kube-scheduler measures plugins in 10% of scheduling cycles, so rare slow calls can be missed. All profiles together, the Profile selector does not apply. The 15 slowest are picked anew at every point in time, so lines appear and disappear along the graph.

targets.expr: topk(15, histogram_quantile(0.99, sum by (le, plugin, extension_point) (rate(scheduler_plugin_execution_duration_seconds_bucket{job="kube-scheduler", node=~"$node"}[$__rate_interval]))))

panels.title: Goroutines in flight by operation
panels.description: Background work of the leader in flight: `binding` counts pods being bound, `prioritizing_extender` counts scoring requests to extenders. `binding` grows when PreBind or Bind is slow, e.g. while volumes are provisioned. Growing `binding` with flat Pods scheduled means binding is stuck: check PreBind and Bind in Extension point duration p99.

targets.expr: sum by (operation) (scheduler_goroutines{job="kube-scheduler", node=~"$node"} * on (instance) group_left () (max by (instance) (leader_election_master_status{job="kube-scheduler", name="kube-scheduler"}) == 1))

panels.title: Scheduler cache
panels.description: Objects the leader keeps in memory: `nodes`, `pods` and `assumed_pods` (placed by the scheduler, binding not confirmed yet). `nodes` matches the number of nodes in the cluster; a deleted node stays until its pods are gone. `assumed_pods` returns to 0 after a burst; a value that stays above 0 means binding is slow: check Goroutines in flight by operation.

targets.expr: sum by (type) (scheduler_cache_size{job="kube-scheduler", node=~"$node"} * on (instance) group_left () (max by (instance) (leader_election_master_status{job="kube-scheduler", name="kube-scheduler"}) == 1))

panels.title: Deciding plugin share

targets.expr: sum by (plugin) (rate(scheduler_decision_deciding_plugin_total{job="kube-scheduler", node=~"$node", profile=~"$profile"}[$__rate_interval])) / ignoring (plugin) group_left () sum (rate(scheduler_decision_deciding_plugin_total{job="kube-scheduler", node=~"$node", profile=~"$profile"}[$__rate_interval]))

panels.title: Deciding plugin over the time range
Score margin of the winner
panels.description: How close each decision was: total score of the chosen node minus the score of the runner-up (the best other node that passed the filters). A small margin means a close call: a minor change in node load flips the choice. Only decisions made by scoring count, ties with margin 0 included; pods placed on the only fitting node, on a nominated node or by node hint have no runner-up and are left out. With percentageOfNodesToScore below 100 the runner-up is the best of the scored subset. Simulations and pods placed by the pod group cycle (Kubernetes 1.36+) are not counted.

panels.title: Feasible nodes per decision
panels.description: How many nodes passed all filters for a placed pod; `max bucket` is the largest value seen, rounded up to the histogram bucket boundary. The dashed line is the number of nodes the scheduler knows: feasible nodes far below it mean filters (affinity, taints, free resources, extenders) narrow the choice. Pods placed on a nominated node or by node hint tried one node and are left out. With percentageOfNodesToScore below 100 the scheduler stops searching after enough feasible nodes, so the count is relative to that subset. Simulations and pods placed by the pod group cycle (Kubernetes 1.36+) are not counted.

panels.title: Configured extenders
panels.description:
Extenders in the scheduler configuration, as reported by every replica.

- Name: the KubeSchedulerWebhookConfiguration of the extender, with `/<n>` added when it has several webhooks. An extender configured without one shows its URL here.
- Filter, Prioritize, Preempt, Bind: the request path for each verb; empty means the extender does not serve it.
- Weight: multiplier of the extender scores.
- Failure policy: with `Fail` a failing extender fails the scheduling attempt, with `Ignore` the scheduler goes on without it.
- Replicas: how many replicas report this exact configuration. Two rows for one extender mean the replicas run different configurations, which is normal only during a rollout.

targets.expr: count by (extender, url, filter_verb, prioritize_verb, preempt_verb, bind_verb, weight, ignorable) (scheduler_extender_info{job="kube-scheduler", node=~"$node", extender=~"$extender"})

panels.title: Requests by extender and verb
panels.description: Requests per second from kube-scheduler to each extender by verb (filter, prioritize, preempt, bind), any result. Requests skipped while the circuit breaker is open are in Circuit breaker openings and skipped requests. Calls made by simulations are not counted.

targets.expr: sum by (extender, verb) (rate(scheduler_extender_request_duration_seconds_count{job="kube-scheduler", node=~"$node", extender=~"$extender", result!="skipped"}[$__rate_interval]))

panels.title: Error ratio by extender and verb
panels.description: Share of requests to an extender that failed: timeout, connection error, HTTP code other than 200, unreadable answer, or an error reported in the answer. Above the yellow line: see the kind of failure in Errors by result. For an extender with failure policy Fail every error fails the scheduling attempt (see Attempt errors); with Ignore, 10 unanswered filter or prioritize requests in a row (timeout, connection, HTTP status, unreadable answer; defaults) open the circuit breaker, an error the extender reports in its answer does not count.

targets.expr: (sum by (extender, verb) (rate(scheduler_extender_request_duration_seconds_count{job="kube-scheduler", node=~"$node", extender=~"$extender", result!~"success|skipped"}[$__rate_interval])) or 0 * sum by (extender, verb) (rate(scheduler_extender_request_duration_seconds_count{job="kube-scheduler", node=~"$node", extender=~"$extender", result!="skipped"}[$__rate_interval]))) / sum by (extender, verb) (rate(scheduler_extender_request_duration_seconds_count{job="kube-scheduler", node=~"$node", extender=~"$extender", result!="skipped"}[$__rate_interval]))

panels.title: Request latency p50 / p99
panels.description: Time of one request to an extender, from preparing the request to the parsed answer, by extender and verb, any result. Dashed lines are p50, solid lines p99. p99 near the extender httpTimeout means requests start to time out: check `timeout` in Errors by result. Every filter and prioritize request adds to Scheduling attempt duration.

targets.expr: histogram_quantile(0.5, sum by (le, extender, verb) (rate(scheduler_extender_request_duration_seconds_bucket{job="kube-scheduler", node=~"$node", extender=~"$extender", result!="skipped"}[$__rate_interval])))

histogram_quantile(0.99, sum by (le, extender, verb) (rate(scheduler_extender_request_duration_seconds_bucket{job="kube-scheduler", node=~"$node", extender=~"$extender", result!="skipped"}[$__rate_interval])))

panels.title: Errors by result
panels.description: Failed requests per second by kind: `timeout` (the extender httpTimeout was reached), `error` (connection failed or the request could not be sent), `status` (HTTP code other than 200), `decode` (the answer is not valid JSON), `extender_error` (the extender answered with an error message). `timeout` points to a slow extender, see Request latency p50 / p99; `error` points to the network or to extender pods being down.

panels.title: Request phases p99 (successful requests)
panels.description: Where a successful request to an extender spends time, 99th percentile per phase: `encode` prepares the request, `conn` waits for a connection, `write` sends the body, `wait` lasts until the first byte of the answer (the extender's own processing), `read` reads and parses the answer. Large `wait` means the extender is slow; large `conn` means connections are not reused. Quantiles do not add up, so the lines are not stacked. All selected extenders and verbs together: pick one extender in the Extender selector for its own breakdown.

panels.title: Filter answers: nodes by outcome
panels.description: Nodes per second in extender filter answers: `passed` the node fits, `failed` rejected but may fit later, `unresolvable` rejected and evicting pods from this node does not help. Mostly `failed` or `unresolvable` means the extender rejects most nodes: see `Extender` in Unschedulable pods by plugin.

panels.title: Circuit breaker state
panels.description: Circuit breaker of each extender with failure policy Ignore. After 10 failed filter or prioritize requests in a row (defaults) kube-scheduler stops calling the extender for 30 seconds, then sends one probe request. `open`: the extender is skipped, so its filter and scores do not affect placements. Extenders with failure policy Fail have no breaker and are not listed.

panels.title: Circuit breaker openings and skipped requests
panels.description: Bars: how many times the circuit breaker opened in each interval; a failed probe opens it again and counts too. Lines (right axis): requests per second skipped while the breaker is open. Repeated bars mean the extender keeps failing: check Errors by result.

targets.expr: sum by (extender, verb) (rate(scheduler_extender_request_duration_seconds_count{job="kube-scheduler", node=~"$node", extender=~"$extender", result="skipped"}[$__rate_interval]))

panels.title: Placements dropped
panels.description: kube-scheduler tells an extender with sendPlacements enabled which pods it has just placed, together with the next prioritize request. Dropped placements were never sent: `overflow` more than 1000 were waiting, `expired` waited longer than 30 seconds for a prioritize request. Any value above 0 means the extender scored pods without knowing about earlier placements, so a burst of pods may land on the same nodes.

panels.title: Simulation requests by code
panels.description: Requests per second to the simulate endpoint of kube-scheduler by HTTP code. Each replica runs one simulation at a time; `429` means another simulation was running on that replica and the client has to retry. While a simulation runs on the leader, real scheduling waits: see Simulation duration.

panels.title: Simulation duration
panels.description: How long one simulation runs, by filter mode: `filters=first` reports the first failing filter per node, `filters=all` reports every failing filter and is slower. Dashed lines are p50, solid lines p99. While a simulation runs on the leader, real scheduling waits, so this is also the delay a simulation adds to pods being scheduled.

panels.title: Simulation lock wait p99
panels.description: 99th percentile of how long a simulation waits before it starts: simulations and real scheduling take turns. High values mean simulations wait for long scheduling cycles: check Scheduling attempt duration.

panels.title: CPU usage and request
panels.description: CPU used by the kube-scheduler container on each master node (solid) and its CPU request (dashed), in millicores (1000 = one core). kube-scheduler has no CPU limit, so usage above the request is allowed. It slows scheduling only when the node CPU is busy: see CPU pressure.

panels.title: CPU pressure
panels.description: Share of time the kube-scheduler container waited for CPU (`waiting` lines). kube-scheduler has no CPU limit, so this is not throttling: it waits because the node CPU is busy and its small CPU request gives it a small share. Every wait stretches scheduling cycles and extender calls, see Scheduling attempt duration. `waiting` needs cgroup v2 and Kubernetes 1.34+; `throttled` lines appear only if a CPU limit is set.

targets.expr: sum by (node) (rate(container_cpu_cfs_throttled_periods_total{namespace="kube-system", container="kube-scheduler", node=~"$node"}[$__rate_interval])) / sum by (node) (rate(container_cpu_cfs_periods_total{namespace="kube-system", container="kube-scheduler", node=~"$node"}[$__rate_interval]))

panels.title: Memory working set and request
panels.description: Working set memory of the kube-scheduler container on each master node (solid) and its memory request (dashed). kube-scheduler keeps all nodes and pods in memory, so memory grows with the cluster size. Standby replicas hold the same data, so similar memory on all replicas is normal.

title: Scheduling
